core_principles.text: Improving awareness of lumbar spine position and thoracic spine mobility can help improve trunk stability during a push-up.
A multiplanar exercise approach combining anti-extension and anti-rotation training can help improve trunk stability during a push-up.

specific_findings.text: In a pilot study of active females, a six-week multiplanar trunk stability intervention resulted in 9 of 20 participants (45%) improving their Trunk Stability Push Up (TSPU) score to ≥2.

consequences.text: Poor trunk stability is a risk factor commonly associated with lower extremity injuries, particularly in females.

core_principles.text: Maintaining a neutral lumbar spine position and control is necessary to prevent anterior pelvic tilt and trunk lag during the push-up.
Single plane, anti-extension exercises can be utilized to encourage the maintenance of neutral lumbar spine positioning during anteriorly directed forces.

common_mistakes.text: Anterior pelvic tilt and trunk lag are common errors where the trunk fails to lift as a single unit during the push-up.

specific_findings.text: Anderson et al. reported that 69% (n=20/29) of high school females failed the Trunk Stability Push Up (TSPU) compared to only 13% (n=4/31) of males.
More than 60% (n=65/108) of active females failed the Trunk Stability Push Up (TSPU) compared to less than 10% (n=10/101) of active males.
The scoring of the Trunk Stability Push Up (TSPU) test demonstrates excellent inter-rater reliability (kw=0.82) and fair to good intra-rater reliability (k=0.68).

consequences.text: Failing to maintain a neutral lumbar spine position during a push-up results in anterior pelvic tilt and trunk lag, indicating impaired trunk stability.

core_principles.text: Position the hands under the shoulders with the thumbs at the height of the clavicles during the start position of the push-up.
Push up from the floor as a unit, keeping the shoulders and hips level.
Performing the trunk stability push-up requires coordinated movement between the upper body, trunk, and pelvis to lift the body as a single unit.
Trunk stability for the push-up can be improved using a combination of anti-extension and anti-rotation exercises that progress in postural demand.

common_mistakes.text: Failing to lift the body as a single unit due to a lack of coordinated movement between the upper body, trunk, and pelvis.
Failing to complete the push-up by only rising one to two inches from the floor due to insufficient upper body strength.

specific_findings.text: In a study of active females, 45% of participants passed the Trunk Stability Push-Up (TSPU) post-intervention, with many of those who failed only able to rise one to two inches from the floor.
All subjects in the study scored a 3 bilaterally on the shoulder mobility pattern, indicating that upper quarter mobility restrictions did not contribute to poor TSPU performance.
A greater proportion of subjects with high Beighton scores of four or greater passed the TSPU at posttest compared to subjects with low scores of zero to three.

consequences.text: Systemic hypermobility impacts ligamentous integrity, which can lead to poor global stability during movement patterns.
